title: Train in private
hook: train in private: drink water in the heat and tell no one (Discourses 3.12)

segments.voice: Yesterday: nosos, the fever as practice, and your line, resting well is the practice. How did you carry whatever your body brought you? Day four hundred twenty, the end of the week.

The ice bath video. The five a.m. run, posted at five-oh-two. The photo of the green juice and the caption about discipline. There's a whole economy now of being seen doing hard things. Some of it is genuinely inspiring. Some of it is mostly about being seen. Epictetus warned about a version of this in his own day, philosophers staging feats of endurance, and he had a test for telling the two apart. Today: askēsis.
screen: `THE ICE BATH VIDEO.` → `POSTED AT FIVE-OH-TWO.` → `A TEST TO TELL THEM APART.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter twelve, on training. Epictetus starts by ruling things out. Don't train with stunts that are strange or showy, he says, or we philosophers will be no different from street performers. Walking a tightrope is hard and dangerous, but that's no reason to practice it. Train where it's useful: in what you want and what you avoid. Then he gets pointed. There were philosophers who hugged cold statues in winter to show how tough they were; the story is told of the Cynic Diogenes. Don't, he says. If you want to train your endurance, do it for yourself, not for the people watching. And here's the exercise. When you're hot and very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. Notice the detail: you don't even get to swallow it. The water is right there, in your mouth, and you let it go. Then he adds a smaller version. If you've given up wine, don't go around announcing, I only drink water. The moment you announce it, part of the training can turn into a performance, and the performance takes the reward. Training in private keeps the reward where it belongs: in you, getting stronger. It's not that sharing is always wrong. It's a test. Would you still do it if no one ever knew? Look back at the week: show me one, no scorekeeping, real beauty, three fields, found doing this, this too trains. And today, privately.
screen: `NO STUNTS, NO TIGHTROPES.` · `DON'T HUG THE COLD STATUES.` · `A MOUTHFUL OF WATER, SPAT OUT.` · `WOULD YOU DO IT IF NO ONE KNEW?` · then, large: `PRIVATELY.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Choose one small piece of training you could do today that no one will ever see: skipping a second helping, not checking your phone for an hour, holding back a complaint, waking a few minutes early to sit like this. Something real, but small. Picture yourself doing it. Then picture the urge to mention it afterward, and letting that urge pass too. Keep it between you and you. The bell holds the time.
Askēsis. Greek for training: Epictetus' rule for practice, no stunts, no announcements; take the cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
Your line: privately. Train one thing today that no one will know about, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day four hundred twenty, and a week done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners keep at least one discipline entirely private, following Epictetus' advice to train for themselves rather than for an audience.

fork.setup: you're hot and very thirsty, and you want to train your self-control. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: drink slowly, in public, so people learn from you.
take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
go without water all day and post about it.
fork.reveal: the exercise is small, real and completely private: the reward stays in you, not in the audience.

original.note: Greek askēsis: training, exercise (our word ascetic comes from it); the subject of Discourses 3.12.

trapdoor: what you thought: discipline means doing hard things.
what it means: useful training, done privately, for yourself and not for an audience.
what a scholar hears: askēsis was also the athlete's word for training, and 3.12's target is philosophers who staged endurance feats, like hugging statues in winter, a habit told of Diogenes.
recall: the student who wrote it down
lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny

notes: Discourses 3.12 paraphrased: no unnatural or showy training (tightrope walking, like jugglers); don't embrace statues; 'if you wish to train for yourself, when you're thirsty take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one'; 'I drink water' not to be announced. Confirm.
The index hook says 'drink water in the heat'; the text has the water spat out. The script follows the text; consider updating the outline hook.
Diogenes Laertius 6.23 for Diogenes hugging bronze statues in winter; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer claims Epictetus watched philosophers performing 'in the street'; statue-hugging attributed to Diogenes (the cited Diogenes Laertius 6.23) rather than to 'philosophers in his day'; the 'performance takes the reward' line is now the script's reading, not attributed to Epictetus; added Enchiridion 47, which has both the 'I drink water' and the cold-water advice (confirm whether 3.12 itself has the 'I drink water' line or only Ench. 47 / Disc. 3.14); trapdoor's 'began as' etymology softened.
